difficultyReason: Scientific/medical argument where the correct answer confirms a load-bearing assumption about a study's control conditions. Distractors are topically plausible but address neighboring claims or introduce irrelevant comparisons.
stimulus: A clinical trial tested whether a new antibiotic reduced recovery time from bacterial pneumonia. Patients who received the antibiotic recovered, on average, four days faster than patients who did not. The researchers concluded that the antibiotic itself was responsible for the faster recoveries.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The antibiotic has been shown to be effective against several other bacterial infections besides pneumonia.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients in both the antibiotic group and the control group received the same standard supportive care throughout the trial.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The antibiotic is less expensive to manufacture than most currently approved antibiotics for pneumonia.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some patients who did not receive the antibiotic also recovered within the average time recorded for the antibiotic group.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bacterial pneumonia is more common in elderly patients than in younger adults.

explanations.correct: The argument's conclusion rests on the antibiotic — not confounding differences in care — causing faster recovery. Confirming that both groups received identical supportive care rules out the alternative that better ancillary treatment explains the difference, directly strengthening the causal claim.
explanations.A: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap: effectiveness against other infections does not bear on whether the antibiotic caused the specific outcome in this trial.
explanations.B: Correct. Rules out the alternative explanation that differential care — rather than the antibiotic — produced the observed difference.
explanations.C: Irrelevant: manufacturing cost has no bearing on whether the antibiotic caused faster recovery.
explanations.D: This actually weakens the inference slightly by suggesting recovery without the antibiotic is possible within the same timeframe.
explanations.E: Unwarranted comparison: demographic epidemiology of pneumonia does not address the causal mechanism within the trial.

difficultyReason: Economics argument requiring the correct answer to close an analogy gap between two different market contexts. Distractors include a plausible-but-irrelevant statistic and a choice that strengthens a neighboring claim.
stimulus: A city government is considering capping rents on residential apartments, citing the success of a similar policy in a neighboring city where median rents fell by twelve percent within two years of implementation. Critics argue the cities are too different for the comparison to hold, because the neighboring city has a much larger rental housing stock. The policy's proponents contend the cap would still reduce rents here.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the proponents' contention?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rent control policies have been attempted in several countries with widely varying outcomes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The neighboring city's rental housing stock has grown by fifteen percent since the policy was introduced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Studies of cities with small rental housing stocks show that rent caps reduce median rents as effectively as in cities with large stocks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city government has successfully capped prices in the commercial real estate sector in the past.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The median income of renters in the two cities is approximately the same.

explanations.correct: The critics' objection is that housing-stock size makes the comparison invalid. Evidence that rent caps work equally well in small-stock cities directly closes that analogy gap and supports the proponents' claim.
explanations.A: Accurate-but-irrelevant: varying outcomes globally does not address whether the cap will work in this specific city.
explanations.B: Strengthens a neighboring claim about the neighboring city's housing supply, not the proponents' contention about this city.
explanations.C: Correct. Directly answers the critics' objection by showing that stock size does not impair the policy's effectiveness.
explanations.D: Unwarranted comparison: commercial real estate price caps operate under different mechanisms than residential rent control.
explanations.E: Irrelevant: income parity does not bear on whether the policy mechanism will reduce rents regardless of stock size.

difficultyReason: Environmental science argument with a causal conclusion about pollution source. Correct answer rules out an alternative pollution source. Distractors include a choice that merely confirms the pollution exists and one that addresses a different conclusion.
stimulus: Elevated mercury levels were detected in fish sampled from a river downstream from a coal-fired power plant. No such elevation was found in fish sampled from the same river upstream from the plant. The environmental agency concluded that the power plant's emissions are responsible for the mercury contamination in the downstream fish.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mercury contamination in fish poses a well-documented health risk to humans who consume them regularly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The power plant has been operating at the same capacity for the past decade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There are no other industrial facilities, mining operations, or known natural mercury deposits between the upstream and downstream sampling sites.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Coal-fired power plants in other regions have been linked to elevated mercury levels in nearby waterways.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The downstream fish samples were collected during the same season as the upstream samples.

explanations.correct: The agency's causal claim requires that no other source between the two sampling points explains the downstream elevation. Ruling out all other industrial, mining, and natural sources between those points directly supports the conclusion that the power plant is responsible.
explanations.A: Accurate-but-irrelevant: health risks of mercury do not bear on whether the plant caused this particular contamination.
explanations.B: Irrelevant to source attribution; operational consistency does not rule out alternative pollution sources.
explanations.C: Correct. Eliminates alternative explanations for the downstream elevation, strengthening the causal inference.
explanations.D: Strengthens a general claim about coal plants and mercury, not the specific causal conclusion about this plant and this river.
explanations.E: Controls for seasonal variation in sampling method — useful but a minor methodological point that does not rule out alternative pollution sources, which is the critical gap.

difficultyReason: Technology/linguistics argument where the correct answer confirms a key mechanism linking the premise to the conclusion. Distractors include an opposite answer and an unwarranted comparison.
stimulus: A software company recently released an updated version of its voice-recognition application. Following the update, the number of user complaints about transcription errors dropped by forty percent. The company attributed this improvement to a new machine-learning model incorporated in the update.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the company's attribution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The new machine-learning model was trained on a dataset three times larger than the one used to train the previous model.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Voice-recognition technology in general has improved steadily over the past decade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The update contained no other changes to the application besides the new machine-learning model.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some users continued to report transcription errors even after installing the update.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The company's competitors also released updates around the same time, which reduced errors in their own applications.

explanations.correct: If the update included only the new machine-learning model and nothing else, then the model is the only candidate cause for the improvement, directly supporting the company's attribution.
explanations.A: Confirms a feature of the model but does not rule out that other changes in the update also contributed to the improvement.
explanations.B: Unwarranted comparison: industry-wide improvement trends do not establish that this specific model caused this specific drop in complaints.
explanations.C: Correct. Eliminates all other within-update alternative causes, making the machine-learning model the only viable explanation.
explanations.D: Opposite-answer trap: continued errors among some users is consistent with the update helping but does not strengthen the attribution.
explanations.E: Irrelevant and potentially weakening: competitors' simultaneous improvements suggest industry trends may explain outcomes, not the specific model.

difficultyReason: History/policy argument where the correct answer confirms a load-bearing premise about intent. Distractors include one that strengthens a different conclusion and one that is accurate but irrelevant.
stimulus: Historians have long debated whether the Roman Senate's decision in 59 BCE to grant Julius Caesar an extended military command in Gaul was primarily motivated by a desire to remove a politically dangerous rival from Rome rather than by genuine strategic necessity. Proponents of the rivalry thesis note that Caesar's command was unusually lengthy and that several senators who supported it were known political adversaries of Pompey, Caesar's main rival at the time.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the rivalry thesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rome faced no documented external military threat from Gaul at the time the command was granted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Caesar's campaigns in Gaul ultimately expanded Roman territory significantly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Senate had previously granted extended commands to generals for documented strategic reasons.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Caesar wrote detailed commentaries on his Gallic campaigns that are still read today.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several senators who opposed the extended command were among Caesar's closest political allies.

explanations.correct: The rivalry thesis holds that political rivalry, not strategic necessity, motivated the Senate. Evidence that no genuine military threat existed at the time undermines the strategic-necessity alternative and directly supports the rivalry thesis.
explanations.A: Correct. Eliminates the strategic-necessity explanation, leaving political rivalry as the more plausible motivation.
explanations.B: Irrelevant to motivation: the eventual outcome does not speak to why the command was granted in the first place.
explanations.C: Weakens slightly by suggesting the Senate had legitimate precedent for extended commands, making strategic necessity more plausible.
explanations.D: Accurate-but-irrelevant: the literary legacy of Caesar's commentaries has no bearing on senatorial motivation.
explanations.E: This detail slightly weakens the rivalry thesis by complicating the political picture — if Caesar's allies opposed the command, the pattern of support is less clearly explained by rivalry alone.

difficultyReason: Ethics/policy argument with an implicit analogical assumption. Correct answer confirms the mechanism connecting the policy premise to the moral conclusion. Distractors include a strengthener of a neighboring claim and an opposite answer.
stimulus: A bioethics committee recommended that hospitals be required to obtain explicit written consent from patients before using their anonymized medical records in research studies. The committee argued that patients have a right to control how their personal information is used, even when that information has been stripped of identifying details.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the committee's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Research studies that use anonymized medical records have produced significant medical advances over the past two decades.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients who are informed about research uses of their records are no less willing to consent than patients who are not informed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anonymization techniques used by hospitals do not completely eliminate the possibility of re-identifying individual patients from their records.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Written consent requirements increase administrative burdens for hospital research departments.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most patients are unaware that their records may be used for research purposes.

explanations.correct: The committee argues that patients retain a right to control their information even after anonymization. If anonymization is imperfect and re-identification remains possible, the records are not truly de-personalized — this confirms that the patient's interest in controlling the information persists even after the stripping process, directly strengthening the committee's reasoning.
explanations.A: Opposite-answer trap: benefits of the research practice could be used to argue against requiring consent, weakening the committee's position.
explanations.B: Accurate-but-irrelevant: willingness to consent once informed does not bear on whether consent should be required.
explanations.C: Correct. Bolsters the implicit premise that anonymized records still retain a meaningful connection to the patient, justifying the right-to-control argument.
explanations.D: Weakens the argument by introducing a cost of the proposed requirement.
explanations.E: Somewhat supports the case for informing patients but strengthens the procedural argument for notification rather than the ethical argument for a right to control.

difficultyReason: Linguistics argument with a predictive conclusion. Correct answer confirms a load-bearing premise about the relevant population. Distractors include an unwarranted comparison and a choice that is topically relevant but addresses the wrong claim.
stimulus: A linguist studying language acquisition found that children raised in bilingual households achieve full grammatical proficiency in their second language significantly earlier than children who begin formal instruction in a second language at age seven or older. The linguist predicted that children raised in bilingual households would also demonstrate stronger long-term retention of their second language in adulthood.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the linguist's prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adults who learned a second language early in childhood show greater neural activation in language-processing regions than those who learned it later.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Children in bilingual households are exposed to both languages in a wider variety of social contexts than are students in formal language classes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Early grammatical proficiency in a second language is strongly correlated with stronger retention of that language in adulthood.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bilingual children often outperform monolingual children on tests of cognitive flexibility.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Formal second-language instruction programs vary widely in quality across different school districts.

explanations.correct: The linguist's prediction links early proficiency (the observed advantage) to stronger adult retention. Confirming that early grammatical proficiency directly correlates with adult retention supplies the missing causal bridge, strengthening the prediction.
explanations.A: Confirms a neurological correlate but does not establish that the neural difference translates into stronger retention specifically.
explanations.B: Confirms the mechanism for why bilingual children acquire the language earlier but does not connect early acquisition to long-term retention.
explanations.C: Correct. Directly links the established advantage (early proficiency) to the predicted outcome (adult retention), closing the inferential gap.
explanations.D: Unwarranted comparison: cognitive flexibility advantages are unrelated to second-language retention.
explanations.E: Accurate-but-irrelevant: variation in instructional quality does not bear on the relationship between early proficiency and adult retention.

difficultyReason: Law/policy argument where the correct answer rules out an alternative legal explanation. Distractors include a choice that strengthens a different conclusion and a classic opposite-answer trap.
stimulus: A legal scholar argues that the dramatic increase in patent litigation over the past fifteen years is primarily attributable to the rise of patent assertion entities — companies that acquire patents solely to license or litigate them rather than to manufacture products. The scholar notes that the share of all patent lawsuits filed by such entities rose from twelve percent to nearly sixty percent during this period.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the scholar's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The total number of patents granted by the patent office increased substantially over the same fifteen-year period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patent litigation brought by manufacturing companies did not increase significantly over the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patent assertion entities tend to target smaller technology companies that lack the resources to mount a vigorous defense.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several countries with fewer patent assertion entities have also seen increases in patent litigation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cost of filing a patent lawsuit has declined over the past fifteen years due to procedural reforms.

explanations.correct: The scholar argues that patent assertion entities drove the overall increase. If litigation by manufacturing companies did not increase, the overall rise must be attributable to the entity category that did grow — patent assertion entities — directly supporting the scholar's claim.
explanations.A: Introduces an alternative explanation: more patents could independently drive more litigation, weakening the attribution to assertion entities.
explanations.B: Correct. Rules out the alternative that manufacturing-company litigation also surged, leaving assertion entities as the primary driver of the increase.
explanations.C: Provides detail about litigation targets but does not bear on whether assertion entities caused the overall increase in litigation volume.
explanations.D: Opposite-answer trap: if countries without assertion entities also saw increases, that suggests other factors drive litigation, weakening the scholar's claim.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative explanation for the overall increase — reduced filing costs — rather than supporting the assertion-entity explanation.

difficultyReason: Arts/cultural argument with an analogical conclusion. Correct answer closes the analogy gap. Distractors include an accurate-but-irrelevant historical fact and a choice that strengthens a neighboring but distinct claim.
stimulus: A musicologist argues that the commercial failure of atonal classical compositions in the mid-twentieth century was primarily due to audience unfamiliarity with the style rather than to any intrinsic aesthetic deficit in the music. As evidence, the musicologist cites the initial hostile reception given to now-celebrated Romantic composers such as Beethoven and Wagner, whose works were ultimately embraced once audiences became accustomed to them.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the musicologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atonal compositions that have been repeatedly broadcast on public radio stations have attracted growing and appreciative audiences over time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beethoven and Wagner were both prolific composers who produced works in multiple genres.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The music industry in the mid-twentieth century was dominated by a small number of record labels that preferred commercially safe repertoire.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several atonal composers were also distinguished music theorists who wrote extensively about their compositional methods.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Audiences in the nineteenth century had access to live performances of new compositions far more frequently than modern audiences do.

explanations.correct: The musicologist's analogy predicts that atonal music, like Romantic music, would be embraced once audiences became accustomed to it. Evidence that repeated exposure has already begun producing appreciative audiences for atonal music directly confirms the analogy and supports the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Confirms that increased familiarity with atonal music produces the same reception shift predicted by the Romantic analogy.
explanations.B: Accurate-but-irrelevant: the compositional output of Beethoven and Wagner does not bear on whether unfamiliarity explains the reception of atonal music.
explanations.C: Introduces an alternative explanation — industry gatekeeping — for the commercial failure of atonal music, weakening the unfamiliarity thesis.
explanations.D: Irrelevant: composers' theoretical writings do not address whether audience unfamiliarity drove commercial failure.
explanations.E: Unwarranted comparison: differences in concert-attendance patterns between centuries do not address the unfamiliarity-versus-aesthetic-deficit question.

difficultyReason: Environmental science/policy argument requiring the correct answer to confirm a key empirical premise. Distractors include a strengthener of a subsidiary claim and a classic opposite-answer trap.
stimulus: City planners in a mid-sized metropolitan area proposed expanding the urban tree canopy to reduce the so-called urban heat island effect — the tendency of cities to be significantly warmer than surrounding rural areas due to the prevalence of heat-absorbing surfaces. The planners predicted that increasing tree coverage by twenty percent would lower peak summer temperatures in city centers by up to three degrees Celsius.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the planners' prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Urban trees provide additional benefits such as improved air quality and reduced stormwater runoff.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cities that increased their tree canopy by similar proportions experienced reductions in peak summer temperatures consistent with the planners' estimate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The urban heat island effect is more pronounced in cities with higher population densities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Planting trees in urban areas is significantly more costly than installing reflective roofing materials, which also reduce urban temperatures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The metropolitan area under consideration has a climate that is cooler than that of most cities where tree-canopy studies have been conducted.

explanations.correct: The planners predict a specific temperature reduction from a specific increase in canopy coverage. Evidence that comparable canopy expansions in other cities produced comparable temperature reductions directly confirms the empirical basis for the prediction.
explanations.A: Accurate-but-irrelevant: collateral benefits of urban trees do not bear on the predicted temperature reduction.
explanations.B: Correct. Confirms the load-bearing empirical premise by showing the predicted mechanism has operated as expected in comparable real-world cases.
explanations.C: Strengthens the general claim that cities experience heat island effects but does not address whether tree canopy expansion will achieve the predicted cooling.
explanations.D: Opposite-answer trap: noting that alternative interventions also exist — and may be cheaper — does not support the planners' prediction and could be read as undermining the proposal.
explanations.E: Potentially weakens: if this city is cooler than the study cities, the generalizability of the canopy-cooling findings to this location is less secure.
